UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

             REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF EXELON CORPORATION AND
                       FIRSTENERGY SERVICE COMPANY

        Pursuant to Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 3131 and Rule 7132 of the Rules of Practice

and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), Exelon

Corporation3 and FirstEnergy Service Company4 (together “Exelon and FirstEnergy”) request

rehearing of the Commission’s June 18 Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the

Federal Power Act (“Show Cause Order”)5 insofar as the Commission found that PJM’s Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) appears to be unjust and unreasonable without new

transmission services that would be available to “large load” customers, specifically what the

Show Cause Order refers to as “flexible large loads.”6 The Commission’s findings that the PJM

Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable without these new transmission service options is

arbitrary and capricious and not based upon reasoned decision making.

           In the Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily found that PJM’s Tariff appears

to be unjust and unreasonable because it “does not include transmission services that reflect

Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of flexible large loads that are willing

and able to limit their use of the transmission system under certain conditions.”7 The Commission

noted that the existing transmission services in PJM consist of Network Integration Transmission

Service and firm and non-firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service. While the Commission stated

that these remain just and reasonable options, the Commission directed PJM to address whether

its Tariff remains just and reasonable without allowing Eligible Customers taking transmission

service on behalf of “flexible large loads” the option of taking one or more of the three new

transmission services that the Commission directed in its December 18, 2025 order on Co-Located

Load in PJM.8

          Exelon and FirstEnergy seek rehearing of these findings for the same reasons they sought

rehearing of the December 18 Co-Located Load Order’s requirement to adopt these new

transmission services for Co-Located Load customers. As with the December 18 Co-Located Load

Order, the purported purpose of the Commission’s findings at issue here is to improve the

availability of service to new large load customers and ensure that service to such customers does

not impose unnecessary costs on existing customers. But the creation of these new forms of

transmission service will not hasten or improve service and instead merely reduce transmission

charges for large loads at the expense of other customers. Requiring new transmission services

for “flexible large loads” or other large load customers will not resolve any actual inadequacy in

           II.        The Burden Under FPA Section 206 Has Not Been Met: The Existing Rate Has
                      Not Been Shown To Be Unjust And Unreasonable.

           The FPA requires that the rates and charges of a public utility “in connection with the

transmission or sale of electric energy subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, and all rules

and regulations affecting or pertaining to such rates or charges shall be just and reasonable.”9

“[A]ny such rate or charge that is not just and reasonable is . . . unlawful.”10 Under FPA section

206, the Commission may, by its own motion or upon complaint from a third party, remedy any

“rate [or] charge” or “any rule, regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate [or] charge”

found to be “unjust [or] unreasonable.”11 “The burden of proving an unjust or unreasonable rate

rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—that is, the Commission or the third-party

complainant.”12 In other words, a respondent to a FPA section 206 complaint is not required to

make an affirmative showing that its existing rate is still just and reasonable.

           For the reasons below, neither FERC nor any other party have met the burden of

demonstrating that PJM’s current rate is unjust and unreasonable so as to require new forms of

transmission service for flexible large load or other large load customers.

                    Large Loads Are Unable to Obtain Reliable, Timely, And Reasonably Priced
                    Service Using The Existing Network Service Construct. Therefore, the

          Under the APA, the Commission “must examine the relevant data and articulate a

Cause Order regarding the need for new transmission services does not meet this standard.

         The totality of the Commission’s reasoning for requiring that new forms of transmission

service be offered to flexible large loads is set forth in Paragraphs 85-87 of the Show Cause Order,

in which the Commission simply states that there is evidence that flexible large loads can “quickly

and verifiably adjust their consumption in response to system conditions and price signals” and

can “potentially defer or reduce the need for Network Upgrades, among other benefits.”16

         The new transmission service options that the Commission proposes to extend to flexible
